title: SRE standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This page defines Redwood Inference SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook structure. The goal is to provide a consistent, auditable approach that teams can apply to every externally and internally facing service so that we maintain predictable availability, latency, and cost.

Audience
- SRE and platform engineers
- Product and service owners
- On-call responders and incident commanders

Scope
This standard applies to all production services owned by Redwood Inference, including Hosted API endpoints, Dedicated routing services, internal control plane components, and data pipelines used for model telemetry and billing.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

1.1 Principles
- Each production service must have at least one SLO aligned to customer-visible behavior (availability, correctness, or latency).
- SLOs should be easy to measure from production telemetry and correspond to an ownerable metric.
- Error budgets are the operational currency for risk: teams may accept controlled risk while error budget remains.

1.2 SLO taxonomy (recommended)
- Availability SLO: successful requests / total requests (successful = 2xx for API, successful pipeline run for jobs).
- Latency SLO: percentile latency for a critical route (p95 or p99 depending on user impact).
- Correctness SLO: model-quality or integrity checks (e.g., embedding dimensionality, checksum, schema validation).

1.3 Default targets and bucketing
- External, customer-facing APIs: 99.95% availability (monthly) and p95 latency <= 300ms for short-generation endpoints.
- Low-latency internal control-plane endpoints: 99.9% availability.
- Batch jobs and async pipelines: objective defined in SLAs per product (typically 99% within SLT window).

1.4 Measurement and windows
- Primary measurement window = rolling 28 days for alerting and anomaly detection; reporting window = monthly for executive dashboards.
- Use production ingress metrics annotated by serving variant and region. All SLOs must include a clear numerator/denominator and the query used to compute them.

1.5 Alerting and burn rate thresholds
- Warning alert: projected burn rate > 1.5x with estimated budget exhaustion in 72 hours.
- High-priority alert: projected burn rate > 3x with estimated budget exhaustion in 24 hours.
- Hard SLO breach: immediate paging when a validated global outage causes a hard breach (notify on-call + product SLA owner).

1.6 Error budget policy and runbooks
- If a team exhausts their error budget, they must:
  1. Pause risky feature rollouts for the impacted service.
  2. Open an action item list owned by a product or service manager.
  3. Schedule a reliability initiative if the budget is exhausted more than twice in a quarter.

SLO example table (copyable)
| Service | SLO metric | Target (30d) | Measurement | Owner |
| Hosted Text API (generate) | request success rate | 99.95% | sum(successful) / sum(total) by region | api-serving-team |
| Realtime Chat Router | p95 latency (ms) | <= 300ms | p95(latency_ms) | routing-team |
| Embedding Pipeline | job completion within 10m | 99% | count(on_time)/count(total) | embeddings-team |

2) Capacity Planning

2.1 Capacity objectives
- Maintain 99th percentile headroom for user-facing routes such that autoscaling and burst capacity absorb expected spikes without SLO degradation.
- Target steady-state utilization baselines per resource class: GPU inference pools 60-70% (to allow for autoscaler headroom), CPU-backed control plane 55-65%.

2.2 Forecast cadence and inputs
- Quarterly capacity forecast aligned to product roadmap and marketing events. Inputs: historical QPS, growth forecasts, model sequence-length distributions, and new feature traffic models.
- Monthly refresh to detect divergence.

2.3 Emergency capacity playbook
- Steps to increase capacity:
  1. Identify constrained pool and region via capacity dashboard.
  2. Trigger horizontal scale (adjust deployment replica count or autoscaling policy).
  3. If autoscaler cannot recover, apply prioritized capacity rules: emergency bursts for paid customers, degrade lower-tier model variants, enable cache-only responses for non-critical routes.
  4. Notify SRE lead and product owner.

2.4 Capacity testing and validation
- Run monthly load tests on staging that mirror p95/p99 tail behaviors and longest expected sequence-lengths.
- Include KV cache warm-up scenarios. Store test run configuration as YAML in the service repo and reference in the runbook.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

3.1 Initiative lifecycle
- Post-incident: identify one corrective initiative with a clear owner and target completion date as part of the postmortem.
- Quarterly reliability planning: SRE and product prioritize initiatives based on impact (SLO improvement), effort, and cost savings.

3.2 Metrics for prioritization
- Error budget reduction potential (estimated % increase in available error budget).
- Cost impact (operational cost delta).
- Time-to-value (weeks).

3.3 Example initiatives
- Improve KV cache TTL autosizing to reduce upstream p95 latency by 20%.
- Add targeted instrumentation to surface model warm-start failures causing higher tail latency.
- Implement adaptive batching for long-sequence requests to reduce GPU token cost by 15%.

4) Incident review standards (postmortems)

4.1 Timeline and responsibilities
- Incident acknowledged: initial incident report created in the incident tracker within 2 hours.
- Postmortem draft: owner assigned and draft completed within 72 hours.
- Final postmortem: published and reviewed within 14 days.

4.2 Postmortem structure (required sections)
- Summary (one-paragraph impact statement)
- Timeline of events (UTC timestamps)
- Root cause(s) (clear and specific)
- Contributing factors and mitigating actions taken during the incident
- Detection and escalation timeline
- Corrective actions and owners (with deadlines)
- Learning and follow-ups (including metric gains expected)
- Confirmation of blameless language and retro notes

4.3 Severity taxonomy and outputs
- Sev1: production outage affecting multiple customers or critical SLA breach — full postmortem with action plan.
- Sev2: partial degradation of service — light postmortem + corrective action list.
- Sev3: localized or single-customer impact — incident summary and owner remediation.

5) Operational tooling and dashboards

5.1 Standard dashboards and traces
- Every service must publish the following dashboards: SLO overview, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), error-rate by code, capacity utilization by resource, and a request-sample trace board.
- Tracing must include top-level spans for: ingress validation, routing, model inference, post-processing, and egress.

5.2 Alerting hygiene
- Alerts must be actionable, have a clear runbook link, and include an owner in the alert payload.
- Avoid noisy alerts: require a minimum sustained window (1 minute for high-priority, 5 minutes for warning), and use rate limiting and deduplication at the alerting tier.

5.3 Observability-as-code
- Dashboards, alert rules, and SLO queries should be defined in code (Grafana/Prometheus JSON/YAML) in the service repo. Changes must be PR-reviewed and linked to a ticket.

5.4 Example alert rule (Prometheus-style query)
- Name: Hosted API p95 latency high
- Query: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service, route)) > 0.3
- Annotations: runbook_url, owner_team, paging_level

6) SRE Runbook standards

6.1 Runbook format (required sections)
- Title and scope
- Quick summary and consequences
- Detection signals and Pager conditions
- Immediate mitigation steps (ordered, with exact CLI/console commands where applicable)
- Escalation path with contacts and paging instructions
- Recovery verification steps and metrics to confirm restoration
- Post-incident follow-ups and links to the postmortem template

6.2 Example runbook: High p95 latency on /v1/generate
- Title: High p95 latency — Hosted Text API (/v1/generate)
- Scope: All production regions for the Hosted Text API route used by public customers.
- Detection signals: p95(latency) > 300ms for 5m AND error-rate < 0.5%
- Immediate mitigations:
  1. Check ingress queues and autoscaler: `kubectl get hpa -n api-serving` and `kubectl describe hpa api-generate`
  2. If pods are CPU-bound, increase replica count: `kubectl scale deployment api-generate --replicas=10 -n api-serving`
  3. If GPU pool is saturated, shift routing to lower-cost variant: flip feature flag `routing.use_safe_variant=true` via the feature flag console and confirm traffic shift in tracing.
  4. If latency caused by KV misses, force a cache warm-up on a small percentage: `curl -X POST https://internal-api/caches/warmup?percent=5`
- Escalation: page on-call SRE (pager duty) if mitigations do not restore p95 within 10 minutes. Page product owner if customer SLA at risk.
- Recovery verification: p95 sustained below 300ms for 15 minutes and successful request rate >= 99.9%

6.3 Runbook maintenance
- Runbooks are owned by the service owner and must be reviewed quarterly or after any change to the service topology. Changes to runbooks must be committed to the service repo and linked to the SRE documentation CI job.

7) Governance and compliance

7.1 Ownership and review cadence
- Each service must name an SLO owner and an on-call primary in the service README.
- SRE org will audit SLO coverage and runbook currency quarterly and publish results to the Reliability Dashboard.

7.2 Exceptions
- Services that cannot conform due to external constraints must request an exception using the security-and-compliance exception process. Exceptions are timeboxed and reviewed by the SRE lead and security.

Appendices

A. Sample SLO query (Prometheus)
- numerator: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-serving",status=~"2.."}[5m]))`
- denominator: `sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api-serving"}[5m]))`
- SLO: `numerator / denominator` computed on a 28d rolling window for reporting.

B. Postmortem checklist
- Create incident ticket within 2 hours
- Assign postmortem owner within 24 hours
- Draft completed within 72 hours
- Finalized and reviewed within 14 days
- Track corrective actions in the reliability initiative board

C. Helpful commands and links
- Incident tracker: https://redwood.atlassian.com/incidents
- PagerDuty schedule: https://redwood.pagerduty.com
- SLO dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.com/d/slo-overview
- Example runbook repo: https://git.redwood.com/sre/runbooks

If you are owning an SLO or runbook and need help, contact the SRE on-call channel (#sre-oncall) or email sre@redwood.com.
